MOLECULAR GENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Medical Center
Department of Medical Genetics

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: [redacted name]
DOB: [redacted date]
MRN: [redacted ID]
Sex: Male
Specimen Type: Peripheral blood
Collection Date: [redacted date]
Received Date: [redacted date]
Report Date: [redacted date]

REFERRAL REASON
Diagnostic testing for Fragile X syndrome

CLINICAL INDICATION
Adult male patient referred for molecular genetic testing to evaluate for Fragile X syndrome.

TEST PERFORMED
FMR1 and FMR2 Repeat Expansion Analysis by PCR

METHODOLOGY
Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes. PCR-based assay was performed to detect CGG repeat expansions in the FMR1 gene (FRAXA locus) and GCC repeat expansions in the FMR2 gene (FRAXE locus). Fragment analysis was performed using capillary electrophoresis to determine repeat sizes. This assay detects normal, intermediate, premutation, and full mutation expansions in both genes.

RESULTS

FMR1 (FRAXA) Analysis:
Allele 1: 29 CGG repeats - NORMAL

FMR2 (FRAXE) Analysis:
Allele 1: 16 GCC repeats - NORMAL

REFERENCE RANGES
FMR1 (FRAXA):
- Normal: 6-50 CGG repeats
- Intermediate: 51-60 CGG repeats
- Premutation: 61-200 CGG repeats
- Full mutation: >200 CGG repeats

FMR2 (FRAXE):
- Normal: 6-30 GCC repeats
- Intermediate: 31-60 GCC repeats
- Premutation: 61-200 GCC repeats
- Full mutation: >200 GCC repeats

INTERPRETATION
Molecular genetic testing reveals normal CGG repeat sizes in the FMR1 gene and normal GCC repeat sizes in the FMR2 gene. These results significantly reduce the likelihood of Fragile X syndrome to less than 1%.

LIMITATIONS
This PCR-based assay detects repeat expansions in the FMR1 and FMR2 genes. A small percentage of Fragile X cases may be caused by point mutations, deletions, or other rearrangements within the FMR1 gene that are not detected by this method. If clinical suspicion remains high, additional testing such as FMR1 gene sequencing or deletion/duplication analysis may be considered.

RECOMMENDATIONS
Based on these normal results, the likelihood of Fragile X syndrome is reduced to <1%. However, if clinical features strongly suggest Fragile X syndrome, consider additional molecular testing to detect rare point mutations or rearrangements not identified by repeat expansion analysis.

This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by [redacted location] Medical Center Molecular Genetics Laboratory. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
